content: Cresols are organic compounds that belong to the class of methylphenols. These compounds are both naturally occurring and synthetically produced, and they are categorized as phenols, which are sometimes referred to as phenolics. Depending on the ambient temperature, cresols can exist as either solids or liquids due to their melting points being close to room temperature. Similar to other phenols, cresols undergo slow oxidation when exposed to air for extended periods, and this process often results in impurities that give cresols a yellowish to brownish-red coloration. Cresols emit an odor characteristic of simple phenols, which is often described as resembling a medicinal smell. In terms of chemical structure, a cresol molecule consists of a methyl group attached to the benzene ring of a phenol molecule. There are three structural isomers of cresols, all sharing the molecular formula (CH3)C6H4(OH). These isomers are ortho-cresol (o-cresol), meta-cresol (m-cresol), and para-cresol (p-cresol). These forms can exist independently or as a mixture. Cresols have a variety of applications. They are used as solvents for other chemicals, as disinfectants, and as deodorizing agents. Additionally, they are utilized in the production of specific chemicals designed to eliminate insect pests. Cresol solutions are commonly employed as household cleaners and disinfectants, with one of the most well-known examples being the product marketed under the trade name Lysol. Historically, cresol solutions were used as antiseptics in surgical procedures, but they have largely been replaced by less toxic alternatives. In mid-20th century America, Lysol was also advertised as a disinfecting vaginal douche. Cresols are present in numerous foods, as well as in wood and tobacco smoke, crude oil, coal tar, and brown mixtures such as creosote, cresolene, and cresylic acids, which are used as wood preservatives. Microorganisms in soil and water produce cresols as they break down organic materials in the environment. Xylenols, which are dimethylphenols, can be considered as methylated cresols. Regarding health effects, most exposures to cresols occur at very low levels that are not harmful. However, when cresols are inhaled, ingested, or come into contact with the skin at very high levels, they can be extremely harmful. Documented effects in humans include irritation and burning of the skin, eyes, mouth, and throat; abdominal pain and vomiting; damage to the heart; anemia; liver and kidney damage; facial paralysis; coma; and even death. Inhalation of high levels of cresols over a short period can cause irritation of the nose and throat. Beyond these effects, little is known about the consequences of inhaling cresols at lower levels over prolonged periods. Ingestion of high levels of cresols can lead to kidney problems, burns in the mouth and throat, abdominal pain, vomiting, and effects on the blood and nervous system. Skin contact with high levels of cresols can result in burns and damage to the kidneys, liver, blood, brain, and lungs. Both short-term and long-term studies in animals have demonstrated similar effects from cresol exposure. However, no human or animal studies have shown that cresols negatively impact reproductive ability. The effects of long-term ingestion or skin contact with low levels of cresols remain unknown.
